From experiments to observational panel data

Last week: Randomization ensures treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes

This week: Can we get identification without randomization?

The promise of panel data:

  • Observe units before and after treatment
  • Use pre-treatment trends to infer counterfactual post-treatment outcomes
  • “Parallel trends” replaces randomization

The claim: If treatment and control groups would have followed parallel trends absent treatment, differencing removes time-invariant confounding

Spoiler: This is harder than it looks!

Difference-in-differences

The canonical difference-in-differences

Setup: Two groups (treatment/control), two periods (pre/post)

Pre \((t=0)\) Post \((t=1)\)
Control \((D=0)\) \(\bar{Y}_{00}\) \(\bar{Y}_{01}\)
Treatment \((D=1)\) \(\bar{Y}_{10}\) \(\bar{Y}_{11}\)

The DiD estimator:

\[\hat{\tau}_{DiD} = (\bar{Y}_{11} - \bar{Y}_{10}) - (\bar{Y}_{01} - \bar{Y}_{00})\]

Intuition:

  • First difference: change in treatment group
  • Second difference: subtract change in control group (the counterfactual trend)
  • Result: treatment effect, purged of common time trends

Identification: What does parallel trends buy us?

The fundamental problem: We never observe \(Y_{i1}(0)\) for treated units

Parallel trends assumption:

\[\mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 0]\]

In words: Absent treatment, treated and control groups would have experienced the same average change

What this gives us:

\[\begin{align} \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1] &= \mathbb{E}[Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 1] + \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 0] \\ &= \text{(observed)} + \text{(observed)} \end{align}\]

The counterfactual is identified! We can estimate the ATT:

\[\tau_{ATT} = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(1) - Y_{i1}(0) \mid D_i = 1]\]

The hardness of parallel trends

The core problem: Parallel trends is an assumption about counterfactuals

\[\mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i1}(0) - Y_{i0}(0) \mid D_i = 0]\]

We never observe \(Y_{i1}(0)\) for treated units \(\implies\) fundamentally untestable

What we’re really assuming:

  • Treatment and control have the same unobserved time-varying factors
  • Selection into treatment based only on:
    • Time-invariant differences (removed by differencing)
    • Observed time-varying factors (can condition on these)
  • No time-varying unobserved confounders that differ by group

This is strong! Requires that all differential trends are due to treatment, not selection

Testing and falsification

Can we test parallel trends? Not directly, but we can check pre-trends

Pre-trends test: Do treatment and control have parallel trends before treatment?

  • If yes: suggests parallel trends might hold post-treatment
  • If no: parallel trends assumption is likely violated

The logic: If trends differ pre-treatment, why would they be parallel post-treatment?

Limitations:

  • Pre-trends can pass even when parallel trends fails
    • Example: Firms change behavior before policy announcement, masking differential pre-trends
  • Pre-trends can fail even when parallel trends holds
    • Example: Treatment targets units with temporarily low outcomes; pre-trends diverge but would have converged absent treatment
  • Limited pre-treatment periods \(\implies\) low statistical power
  • Absence of evidence \(\neq\) evidence of absence

Bottom line: Pre-trends are good but not determinative of parallel trends

When is parallel trends sensitive to functional form? (Roth and Sant’Anna 2023)

The insight: Parallel trends can hold in one scale but not another

Example: Consider earnings \(Y\) and log earnings \(\log(Y)\)

  • Levels: \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}(0) - Y_{t-1}(0) \mid D=1] = \mathbb{E}[Y_{t}(0) - Y_{t-1}(0) \mid D=0]\)
  • Logs: \(\mathbb{E}[\log Y_{t}(0) - \log Y_{t-1}(0) \mid D=1] = \mathbb{E}[\log Y_{t}(0) - \log Y_{t-1}(0) \mid D=0]\)

These cannot both be true! (except in degenerate cases)

The problem:

  • Parallel trends in levels \(\implies\) constant additive differences
  • Parallel trends in logs \(\implies\) constant multiplicative differences
  • Your choice of scale is an untestable assumption

Why randomization is different: With random treatment assignment, \(D \perp (Y(0), Y(1))\) holds in all functional forms

  • Independence is scale-invariant

When does DiD go wrong?

The setting: Multiple groups, staggered treatment adoption

Two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression:

\[Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \tau D_{it} + \epsilon_{it}\]

The promise: \(\hat{\tau}\) estimates the average treatment effect

The problems:

  1. Heterogeneous treatment effects: If effects vary across groups/time, TWFE is a weighted average with potentially negative weights (De Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille 2020)

  2. Forbidden comparisons: TWFE compares already-treated units to newly-treated units, which violates parallel trends (Goodman-Bacon 2021)

  3. The result: \(\hat{\tau}\) can be biased, even with the sign flipped!

Bottom line: Basic TWFE with staggered adoption can be perilous

(Goodman-Bacon 2021)

Three timing groups

Early group \(k\), late group \(\ell\), never-treated group \(U\). Effects are constant: \(10\) for \(k\), \(15\) for \(\ell\).

TWFE is an average of 2x2s

Theorem: \(\hat{\tau}_{TWFE} = \sum s \cdot \hat{\beta}^{2\times 2}\) over all four comparisons, with weights \(s \geq 0\), \(\sum s = 1\), set by group sizes and the variance of \(D_{it}\) in each window

The forbidden comparison

Panel D uses the already-treated group \(k\) as the control for \(\ell\). Under parallel trends:

\[\hat{\beta}^{2\times 2, \ell}_{k\ell} \to ATT_\ell(\text{POST}) - \big[ATT_k(\text{POST}) - ATT_k(\text{MID})\big]\]

  • Constant effects: the bracket is zero, and panel D is fine
  • Effects that grow with exposure: the growth in \(k\)’s effect is subtracted from \(\ell\)’s

  • Identical counterfactuals; the effect grows linearly from adoption
  • In POST\((\ell)\) both groups grow equally fast, so the gap stops widening
  • Panel D sees the gap shrink relative to MID: an effect \(\leq 0\)

The decomposition, simulated

Parallel trends holds. Every unit’s effect is positive and grows by \(1\) per period of exposure.

Every weight is positive; the later vs earlier 2x2s go negative. This is where the negative weights of (De Chaisemartin and d’Haultfoeuille 2020) come from

(Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021)

Modern solutions

The key insight: Avoid forbidden comparisons by using never-treated units as controls (Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021; Sun and Abraham 2021)

Group-time ATTs: Estimate treatment effects for each cohort \(g\) at each time \(t\):

\[ATT(g,t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{it}(1) - Y_{it}(0) \mid G_i = g]\]

where \(G_i\) is the period when unit \(i\) first receives treatment

Aggregation: Combine group-time ATTs to get target parameters:

  • Overall ATT: weighted average across all \((g,t)\)
  • Dynamic effects: average by event time \(t - g\)
  • Group-specific effects: average over time for each \(g\)

Advantages: Valid inference, handles heterogeneity, avoids negative weights

Identifying \(ATT(g,t)\)

No anticipation: \(Y_{it} = Y_{it}(0)\) for all \(t < G_i\)

Parallel trends, cohort by cohort: with \(C_i = 1\) for never-treated units,

\[\mathbb{E}[Y_t(0) - Y_{t-1}(0) \mid G = g] = \mathbb{E}[Y_t(0) - Y_{t-1}(0) \mid C = 1]\]

Then each \(ATT(g,t)\) is one clean 2x2, with base period \(g - 1\):

\[ATT(g,t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid G = g] - \mathbb{E}[Y_t - Y_{g-1} \mid C = 1]\]

  • Controls are never treated: no already-treated unit is ever a control
  • Alternative: use the not yet treated (\(G_i > t\)) as controls, a larger comparison group
  • With covariates, each 2x2 can be estimated by outcome regression, IPW, or the doubly robust estimator from Week 4

Group-time ATTs in a picture

Same kind of growing effect, three cohorts plus a never-treated group

  • Points before \(g - 1\) are placebo estimates: a pre-trends check, cohort by cohort

Aggregating group-time ATTs

The analyst chooses the weights, and they are never negative

By event time (an event study), over the cohorts observed \(e\) periods after adoption:

\[\theta(e) = \sum_{g} \Pr(G = g \mid g + e \leq T)\, ATT(g, g + e)\]

By cohort:

\[\theta(g) = \frac{1}{T - g + 1} \sum_{t \geq g} ATT(g, t)\]

Overall: average \(\theta(g)\) with weights \(\Pr(G = g \mid G \leq T)\)

  • Long horizons \(e\) come from early cohorts only: the mix of cohorts changes with \(e\)

Event study: group-time ATTs vs TWFE

Same simulated panel as the decomposition: true ATT \(6.4\), TWFE \(1.3\)

(Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller 2010)

Synthetic controls: Focusing on parallel trends

The motivation: What if parallel trends doesn’t hold for any single control unit?

Classic example: Effect of California’s tobacco control program (Prop 99, 1988) (Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller 2010)

  • One treated unit (California)
  • Many potential control states (almost 50, in fact)
  • But no single state is a good match for California

The insight: Create a synthetic California from other states

The synthetic control method

Setup: One treated unit, \(J\) control units (the “donor pool”)

Goal: Find weights \(w_j \geq 0\) with \(\sum_j w_j = 1\) such that:

\[\sum_{j=2}^{J+1} w_j Y_{jt} \approx Y_{1t} \quad \text{for all pre-treatment periods } t < T_0\]

How to find weights: Solve optimization problem

\[\min_{w} \sum_{t<T_0} \left(Y_{1t} - \sum_j w_j Y_{jt}\right)^2 \quad \text{subject to } w_j \geq 0, \sum_j w_j = 1\]

  • Why \(w_j \geq 0\)?
  • Why \(\sum_j w_j = 1\)?

Identification: If it matches trends pre-treatment, maybe also post-treatment?

Why synthetic control works

Key assumption: The outcome follows a factor model

\[Y_{it} = \delta_t + \theta_t Z_i + \lambda_t \mu_i + \epsilon_{it}\]

where \(\delta_t\) are time effects, \(Z_i\) are observed covariates, \(\mu_i\) are unobserved factors

If weights reproduce:

  • Pre-treatment outcomes
  • Pre-treatment covariates
  • And we have enough pre-treatment periods

Then: The weighted control units have the same \(\mu_i\) as the treated unit

Result: \(\sum_j w_j^* Y_{jt}\) is an unbiased estimate of \(Y_{1t}(0)\) post-treatment

Extensions: Augmented SC (Ben-Michael, Feller, and Rothstein 2021) adds outcome modeling for robustness

Synthetic control as an event study

  • Before: the SC gap sits in the placebo band; DiD shows a pre-trend
  • After: the SC gap tracks the true effect; DiD gets the sign wrong
  • Inference: is the treated gap extreme among the donor placebos?

Synthesis

The evolution of diff-in-diff methods

Classic DiD (pre-2000s): 2x2 design with parallel trends assumption

  • Simple and intuitive, but limited to two groups and two periods

TWFE era (2000s-2010s): Panel data with unit and time fixed effects

  • Became the workhorse of applied econometrics

The reckoning (2018-2021): Discovery of fundamental problems

  • Forbidden comparisons, negative weights, functional form sensitivity

Modern solutions (2020s): New estimation strategies

  • Group-time aggregation, synthetic controls, sensitivity analysis

The lesson: Even “simple” methods hide complex assumptions
